result.abstractText: The concurrent impact of chronic psychological stress and sleep disruption on systemic adaptation and hippocampal cytoarchitecture remains poorly understood. This study investigated the neurobiological threshold of compounded stress by exposing male Wistar rats to combined Chronic Unpredictable Mild Stress (CUMS) and Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Deprivation (RSD), specifically chosen over total sleep deprivation due to the unique role of REM sleep in emotional regulation and spatial memory consolidation over 21 days. We evaluated body weight loss, sensorimotor function Open Field Test (OFT), declarative memory Novel Object Recognition (NOR), serum corticosterone, hippocampal malondialdehyde (MDA), and Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF). Results revealed that the combined stress paradigm precipitated significant body weight loss while preserving basal locomotor activity. In contrast to motor preservation, spatial recognition memory was significantly impaired. Biochemically, serum corticosterone and hippocampal MDA levels did not show statistically significant differences across groups. Crucially, while isolated CUMS significantly suppressed hippocampal BDNF protein content and RSD exhibited a similar trend of reduction, the combined paradigm triggered a compensatory neurotrophic rebound, returning BDNF to control baseline levels. However, the localized BDNF rebound did not translate to recovery cognitive performance. These findings suggest a phenomenon of neurobiological dissociation under compounded stress exposure. The organism experiences significant body weight loss and declarative memory impairment, while simultaneously initiating a localized, yet functionally ineffective, compensatory BDNF response in the hippocampus.

result.abstractText:
Background

Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 1 (NOD1) recognizes bacterial peptidoglycan fragments and regulates inflammatory responses. However, its role in perioperative memory performance remains unclear. This study investigated the involvement of NOD1 in the hippocampal CA1 region and gut-related alterations in postoperative memory performance.

Methods

Mice underwent preoperative acute sleep deprivation, anesthesia/surgery, or both. Behavioral testing, hippocampal transcriptomics, fecal metagenomic sequencing, western blotting and immunofluorescence were performed. Iba1 promoter-driven NOD1 knockdown in the hippocampal CA1 region and Lyz1-/- mice were used to investigate the involvement of NOD1 in the hippocampal CA1 region and intestinal lysozyme, respectively.

Results

No statistically significant synergistic or facilitating interaction between sleep deprivation and anesthesia/surgery was detected. Significant main effects were observed in the object location memory test (OLMT) and novel object recognition test (NORT), whereas the Y-maze showed only a post hoc difference between the SD + Sur and Con groups. The reduced postoperative memory performance was accompanied by increased NOD1 expression, an elevated p-p65/p65 ratio and Iba1-related changes in the hippocampal CA1 region, together with gut microbiota dysbiosis and increased ileal expression of lysozyme. Both Iba1 promoter-driven NOD1 knockdown and Lyz1 deficiency reduced NOD1 expression, p65 phosphorylation and Iba1-related changes. Iba1 promoter-driven NOD1 knockdown improved memory performance, whereas Lyz1 deficiency improved OLMT and Y-maze performance and showed a trend toward improved NORT performance.

Conclusions

Hippocampal CA1 NOD1, gut microbiota dysbiosis and ileal lysozyme may contribute to reduced postoperative memory performance associated with preoperative acute sleep deprivation and anesthesia/surgery.

result.abstractText: Sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function by disrupting hippocampal signaling pathways essential for memory formation. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) and lactate, a metabolic byproduct of exercise, have demonstrated potential benefits for brain plasticity, but their protective roles during sleep deprivation remain poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of six weeks of HIIT and lactate administration on memory-related gene expression and spatial learning in sleep-deprived rats. Forty-two male Wistar rats were divided into six groups: Control, Sleep Deprivation (SD), HIIT, HIIT + SD, Lactate, and Lactate + SD. After interventions, sleep deprivation was induced for 48 h. Spatial learning was assessed via the Morris Water Maze test, and hippocampal gene expression of PKA, LIMK, and cofilin was analyzed. The results showed no significant differences in spatial learning performance across groups; however, sleep deprivation caused significant downregulation of key genes involved in memory signaling. Both HIIT and lactate treatments effectively reversed these molecular impairments, notably increasing LIMK expression. These findings highlight the molecular protective effects of HIIT and lactate against sleep deprivation-induced cognitive dysfunction and suggest their potential as non-pharmacological strategies to preserve memory function under sleep loss conditions.
